title: 케이크 다 품절되는 집이잖아  (That Shop Sells Out of Cake)

segments.t: Inside a private dining room at a Korean restaurant, producer Ra Joon-mo and head writer Son Ji-yeon wait nervously for their cast dinner to begin. Veteran actress Youn Yuh-jung walks in beaming over a box of famous cake, completely unaware that the cast is leaving the show. Listen for "pumjeol", meaning 'sold out', and "sugo", used to thank someone for hard work.
나 이 프로 라 피디 때문에 한 거야.
점심때만 돼도 케이크 다 품절되는 집이잖아.
왜 이래? 더 이상 안 볼 사람처럼.
앞으로도 걱정 마. 내가 더 열심히 한다고.
Let's walk through the dinner conversation line by line.
'There is no word yet.' Ji-yeon checks her phone and leads with "ajik", meaning 'yet' or 'still'. "Yeollak" covers a call or message, and "eomneundeyo" trails off with anxious suspense.
'Will everyone come?' Here "dadeul" gathers 'everyone' in the group. Slipping "-si-" inside "osilkkayo" honors the senior actresses she is waiting for.

'Ms. Youn Yuh-jung, please sit here.' In broadcasting, veteran actors are addressed respectfully as "seonsaengnim", literally 'teacher'. Pointing to the seat of honor, Ji-yeon pairs "yeogi", 'here', with "anjeuseyo", 'please sit down'.
'Hello.' Entering the private room, Yuh-jung greets the table with "annyeonghaseyo", the all-purpose polite Korean greeting that works morning, afternoon, or night.
'Teacher, let me pour you a glass.' At a Korean dinner table, offering a drink is a classic sign of respect: "han jan" counts 'one glass', while "badeusiji" warmly urges an elder to accept the pour.
나 이 프로 라 피디 때문에 한 거야.
'I took this show because of Producer Ra.' Speaking casually as the elder at the table, Yuh-jung shortens television program to "peuro" and uses "ttaemune" right after a name to say 'because of'.
'Of course, I know.' Joon-mo agrees right away with "geureomyo", a warm, reassuring 'of course', followed by "aljyo", 'naturally I know'.
'Because we heard you love the cake from this shop.' Ji-yeon points out the gift box using "keikeu" for 'cake' and "joahandago", quoting what they heard she likes.
점심때만 돼도 케이크 다 품절되는 집이잖아.

'Even by lunchtime, this shop sells out of cake.' Impressed, Yuh-jung notes "jeomsimttae", 'lunchtime', and "pumjeol", the store word for 'out of stock'. Notice how "jip", usually 'house', also means a restaurant or bakery in everyday talk.

'Teacher, thank you so much for all your hard work up to now.' Trying to hint at a farewell, Joon-mo says "geudongan", 'during all this time', before "sugo maneusyeosseuminda", the classic salute after finishing a big project together.
왜 이래? 더 이상 안 볼 사람처럼.

'Why are you acting like this? Like people who won't meet anymore.' Sensing his stiff tone, Yuh-jung pushes back with "wae irae", 'what's gotten into you?'. "Deo isang" means 'any longer', paired with "saramcheoreom", 'like people who'.

'No, of course we should see you often.' Losing his nerve, Joon-mo backpedals with "anijyo", 'no, not at all', and "jaju", 'often'. "Bwaeyajyo" comes from "boepda", the humble way to say 'see' or 'meet' an elder.
'Thank you for giving it your all.' He retreats to safe gratitude: "yeolsimhi" means 'wholeheartedly' or 'with real effort', leading into "gamsahamnida", the formal 'thank you'.
앞으로도 걱정 마. 내가 더 열심히 한다고.

'Don't worry going forward either. I told you I will work even harder.' Still convinced she is staying on the cast, Yuh-jung reassures him with "apeurodo", 'in the future too', and "geokjeong ma", a warm casual 'don't worry'. Now let's listen to the whole dinner-table scene straight through.
나 이 프로 라 피디 때문에 한 거야.
점심때만 돼도 케이크 다 품절되는 집이잖아.
왜 이래? 더 이상 안 볼 사람처럼.
앞으로도 걱정 마. 내가 더 열심히 한다고.
You now have "pumjeol" for sold-out treats, "han jan" for pouring a drink, and "geokjeong ma" to tell a friend not to worry. Until next time!
